What is the difference between HTTP GET and HEAD?
rows.gt: HEAD is identical to GET except the server returns only headers and no response body, so it is used to check whether a resource exists or has changed.
rows.a: HTTP GET requests a resource and retrieves its data, while HTTP HEAD requests the same resource but only retrieves the headers without the body of the response. GET is used to fetch content, whereas HEAD is useful for checking metadata or the resource's status without transferring the actual content.

rows.q: What is the difference between HTTP GET and HEAD?
rows.gt: HEAD is identical to GET except the server returns only headers and no response body, so it is used to check whether a resource exists or has changed.
rows.a:
The primary difference between HTTP GET and HEAD is that a GET request retrieves both the header information and the message body of a resource, whereas a HEAD request retrieves only the header information. 

When a client sends a HEAD request, the server returns the same response headers that it would have sent for a GET request—such as the content type, content length, and cache-control directives—but it omits the actual data content. This makes HEAD requests significantly faster and more bandwidth-efficient, making them ideal for checking if a file exists, determining the size of a resource, or validating if a document has been modified since it was last cached, all without the overhead of downloading the entire payload.

rows.q: What is the difference between HTTP GET and HEAD?
rows.gt: HEAD is identical to GET except the server returns only headers and no response body, so it is used to check whether a resource exists or has changed.
rows.a: The core difference is that GET returns the resource's full message body in the response, while HEAD is identical to GET in every other respect—same request headers, same URL, same status code, and same response headers—but the server must not send any message body. In other words, HEAD is a metadata-only request: you get the same headers you would receive from a GET (like Content-Length, Content-Type, Last-Modified, ETag), but the actual content is omitted, saving bandwidth and time. It is commonly used to check whether a resource exists, whether it has changed (via Last-Modified or ETag), or to discover its size without downloading it.

rows.q: What is the difference between HTTP GET and HEAD?
rows.gt: HEAD is identical to GET except the server returns only headers and no response body, so it is used to check whether a resource exists or has changed.
rows.a: HTTP GET requests retrieve a resource from a server and include the response body containing the actual content, such as an HTML page, image, or JSON data. HTTP HEAD requests are identical to GET requests in every way except that the server must not return a message body in the response; it only returns the status line and headers. This makes HEAD useful for checking if a resource exists, verifying when it was last modified, determining its content type or size, or testing link validity without incurring the overhead of downloading the full payload. Both methods are considered safe and idempotent, meaning they should not alter server state and can be repeated without side effects, but HEAD is specifically designed for retrieving metadata about resources efficiently.
